description: We're going to build a health monitoring system for astronauts in space missions.
summary:
Orbit is an offline capable astronaut health tracking prototype developed to help crew members record and review health information during space missions. It includes daily check-ins for heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, sleep, mood, and stress, alongside trend charts, measurement history, and downloadable reports. An experimental camera feature explores contactless pulse estimation.

Orbit addresses the challenge of monitoring health when internet access is limited or unavailable. Records remain on the device, and an offline statistical model learns patterns from previous check-ins to flag unusual measurements. Separate reference-based warnings provide explanations and prompts for medical review.

The project is important because organised, accessible health records can support crew awareness and informed discussions with medical teams during periods of communication delay. Orbit demonstrates a foundation for onboard health monitoring while remaining a prototype: its camera estimates, statistical model, and warning rules require validation before operational or clinical use.
details:
Orbit is an offline-capable astronaut health tracking prototype that brings daily health records, trend analysis, experimental camera monitoring, and measurement advisories into one application.

Users enter available measurements including heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, sleep, mood, and stress through a guided check-in. Orbit stores these records locally, displays changes over time, and allows users to edit entries, export backups, and generate PDF reports. The browser version uses IndexedDB, while the desktop version uses a local SQLite database.

An offline statistical anomaly model learns patterns from at least eight prior dates of comparable measurements. It compares new readings with the recorded baseline and explains unusual changes. Separate reference based rules flag measurements for review, even before sufficient history exists. An experimental camera feature uses facial landmarks and variations in skin colour to estimate pulse; these estimates remain separate from the saved measurements used for advisories.

Orbit’s main benefit is continued access to health information without a continuous internet connection. Its intended impact is to support consistent recordkeeping, crew awareness, and clearer communication with medical teams when mission communications are delayed. It supports human review rather than replacing medical judgment.

We developed Orbit using JavaScript, JSX, React, Vite, and CSS for the interface Rust and Tauri for the desktop application; and Python, OpenCV, MediaPipe, and NumPy for experimental camera processing. Other tools include SQLite, IndexedDB, Recharts, React PDF, Git, and GitHub. Development and testing used a computer and webcam, without requiring dedicated biomedical hardware for the camera prototype.

The project’s creativity lies in combining an offline workflow with explainable personal-pattern detection and experimental contactless sensing. Instead of presenting an unexplained warning, Orbit shows the measurement, date, context, and reason behind each flag.

Our team considered unreliable connectivity, local data storage, backup and recovery, usability, missing measurements, measurement context, and the distinction between simulated and recorded data. We also considered privacy and medical limitations: records are currently unencrypted, the model does not establish a healthy baseline, and the camera estimates and warning rules require qualified validation before clinical or operational use.
dataRefs: NASA — Risk of Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders
